edits.old: A **SiPM** (silicon photomultiplier) is an array of SPADs whose outputs are summed into one analogue signal.
edits.new: A **VCSEL** (vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser) emits from the chip surface, which makes dense laser arrays on one chip easy. A **SPAD** (single-photon avalanche diode) is a photodiode biased above breakdown, so that a single photon can trigger a detectable avalanche, and a **SiPM** (silicon photomultiplier) is an array of SPADs whose outputs are summed into one analogue signal. **FMCW** (frequency-modulated continuous-wave) lidar is the coherent kind: it sweeps its laser frequency and measures range and velocity from the beat between the return and the local oscillator.
edits.why: Defines VCSEL, SPAD and FMCW at first use in §C4d.

where $R$ is the target range, $c$ the speed of light and $\Omega$ the *optical* angular speed, i.e. the rate at which the outgoing beam direction sweeps (for a mirror, twice its mechanical rotation rate, because reflection doubles angles). The formula assumes that $\Omega$ is constant during the flight time. This is the ToF counterpart of the coherent lag angle in §C10.3a (item 6). edits.new:
$$\Delta\theta=\frac{2R\,\dot\theta}{c} \tag{71}$$

where $R$ is the target range, $c$ the speed of light and $\dot\theta$ the *optical* angular speed, i.e. the rate at which the outgoing beam direction sweeps (for a mirror, twice its mechanical rotation rate $\dot\theta_{\rm m}$, because reflection doubles angles). With $\dot\theta$ in °/s, $\Delta\theta$ comes out in degrees; with $\dot\theta$ in rad/s, in radians. The formula assumes that $\dot\theta$ is constant during the flight time. A resonant mirror scanning $\theta(t)=(\Theta_{\rm pp}/2)\sin2\pi ft$, where $\theta(t)$ is the optical beam angle at time $t$, $\Theta_{\rm pp}$ the peak-to-peak optical scan angle and $f$ the resonant frequency, moves fastest mid-sweep. edits.new: - **Optical angular speed.** A 10 Hz spin is $360°\times10=3{,}600$°/s. The AT128 mirror turns at $\dot\theta_{\rm m}=200/60\times360°=1{,}200$°/s, doubled on reflection to $\dot\theta=2{,}400$°/s. Each of its three facets turns through 120° per frame and so sweeps the beam through 240°, of which the 120° field uses half; the frame-average rate $120°\times10\ {\rm Hz}=1{,}200$°/s used for a column sweep in §C10.3a (item 6) is therefore half this active rate. The Falcon K1 polygon turns at 76 rev/s (subsection 2(a)), so $\dot\theta=2\times360°\times76\ {\rm s^{-1}}=54{,}720$°/s, the value in the table; the lower bound used in §C7 and §C7b, $120°\times380\ {\rm s^{-1}}=45{,}600$°/s, assumes that the 120° field fills each facet's whole sweep time. A resonant mirror scanning $\theta(t)=(\Theta_{\rm pp}/2)\sin2\pi f_{\rm mirror}t$, where $\theta(t)$ is the optical beam angle at time $t$, $\Theta_{\rm pp}$ the peak-to-peak optical scan angle and $f_{\rm mirror}$ the resonant frequency, moves fastest mid-sweep. Its time derivative peaks there at $\dot\theta_{\max}=\pi f_{\rm mirror}\Theta_{\rm pp}$:

The same step gives 0.0032° (AT128), 0.073° (polygon at 54,720°/s; 0.091° at 250 m, and 0.061° at the 45,600°/s lower bound),

edits.old: by about $\Omega D/\lambda$ per pass. Here $\Omega$ is the optical angular speed in rad/s, $D$ the beam diameter on the scanner and $\lambda$ the wavelength. That caps the chirp (the FMCW frequency sweep) at roughly the time the beam takes to cross its own width (§C7, scanner-induced Doppler).
edits.new: by about $\Delta f_{\rm scan}\approx\dot\theta D/\lambda$ per pass. Here $\dot\theta$ is the optical angular speed in rad/s, $D$ the beam diameter on the scanner and $\lambda$ the wavelength. A chirp (the FMCW frequency sweep) longer than about $1/\Delta f_{\rm scan}=\lambda/(\dot\theta D)$ is smeared, so that time caps the chirp; it is also the time the beam takes to sweep through one diffraction-limited beamwidth, $\lambda/D$. For a 5 mm beam at 1,550 nm and the Falcon polygon's lower-bound 45,600°/s (796 rad/s), $\Delta f_{\rm scan}=796\ {\rm s^{-1}}\times5\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}/(1.55\times10^{-6}\ {\rm m})\approx2.6$ MHz, which caps the chirp near $1/(2.6\ {\rm MHz})\approx0.39$ µs (§C7, scanner-induced Doppler).
edits.why: Shows the step from frequency spread to chirp cap, says which width is meant, and gives the §C7 number.

edits.old:
- Shrinking the pitch shortens $f$ (30 → 5.7 mm) without the photon penalty it imposes on a SPAD staring array (§C6: 28.5 → 11.5 mm).
  - The difficulty moves to the antenna: contiguous sampling needs each cell's mode to fill most of its pitch. That is why Berkeley's array (a $f\approx5$ mm lens, since $55\ \mu{\rm m}/(0.6\times\pi/180)=5.3$ mm) samples at 0.6° with 0.05° beams (§C10.4).
edits.new:
- Shrinking the pitch shortens $f$ (30 → 5.7 mm) without a photon penalty. In a SPAD staring array the same kind of shrink, from 10.08 to 4 µm SPAD pitch, cuts the f/1.2 entrance aperture from 28.5 to 11.5 mm, about six times less collecting area ($(28.5/11.5)^2=6.1$; §C6).
  - The difficulty moves to the antenna: contiguous sampling needs each cell's mode to fill most of its pitch. Berkeley's array shows the gap. Its lens has $f=55\ \mu{\rm m}/(0.6\times\pi/180)=5.3$ mm, so a 0.05° beam corresponds to a mode only $f\,\theta_{\rm beam}=5.3\ {\rm mm}\times8.7\times10^{-4}\approx4.6\ \mu{\rm m}$ wide in the focal plane, a twelfth of the 55 µm pitch. The array therefore samples at 0.6° with 0.05° beams ($0.6/0.05=55/4.6\approx12$; §C10.4).
edits.why: The §C6 pair is an entrance aperture, not a focal length; the 0.6°/0.05° step is derived.

edits.old:
In short, the reticle is a hard design constraint only for one-cell-per-direction architectures. For the rest, other limits bind first, and chip area matters mainly through yield and cost.

- **Reticle is a real constraint mainly for "one cell per direction" designs at automotive resolution:** staring SPAD arrays and switched FMCW focal-plane arrays.
- For scanned SPAD columns, SiPMs, lasers and continuously steered OPAs, other limits usually bind first: photons, memory, pins, phase control, heat.

edits.old: The exception is near temperature extremes, because a laser's wavelength rises with temperature: a 905 nm edge-emitting laser (EEL) drifts to about 927 nm at +105 °C ($905+0.27\ {\rm nm\,K^{-1}}\times80\ {\rm K}\approx927$ nm, taking 905 nm at 25 °C; 0.27 nm/K is the laser's wavelength temperature coefficient).
edits.new: The exception is at temperature extremes, because a laser's wavelength rises with temperature. A 905 nm edge-emitting laser (EEL), whose wavelength temperature coefficient is 0.27 nm/K, drifts to about 927 nm at +105 °C ($905\ {\rm nm}+0.27\ {\rm nm\,K^{-1}}\times80\ {\rm K}\approx927$ nm, taking 905 nm at 25 °C). That reaches a 940 nm receiver only through a filter wider than about 26 nm ($2\times(940-927)$ nm), at the wide end of the 10–40 nm range.
edits.why: States the consequence of the 927 nm drift.
